title: How to use a scroll frame for cross-stitch
subtitle: Mounting fabric on rods for hands-free stitching and even tension
excerpt: A scroll frame holds cross-stitch fabric taut between two horizontal rods, with the excess fabric rolled up on each rod. Unlike a hoop, it does not leave a ring mark and it keeps the full working width of the fabric accessible without re-hooping. It is the standard tool for larger pieces or for fabric counts above 18ct.
sourceNotes: Scroll frame use documented in cross-stitch publisher guides and Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.
The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: or linen between two rods that can be locked at different heights to adjust the tension. The fabric rolls up on each rod as the stitching advances. For a large piece, only a portion is visible at a time; unrolling one rod and rolling up the other moves the work area forward. The frame itself can rest on a stand or between the knees, freeing both hands for stitching.
Mounting fabric on a scroll frame

Hem the top and bottom edges of the fabric, or attach a webbing tape, so they can be sewn to the rod pockets. The rods have a slot or tape along their length; the fabric attaches along this slot. Some frames use laced tape; others use a cord sewn through eyelets in the fabric margin.

Sew the top edge of the fabric to the top rod pocket with a running stitch in strong thread. Work from the centre outward to both ends, distributing the fabric evenly along the rod. Repeat for the bottom edge on the lower rod.

Insert the rods into the frame sides. Tighten the wing-nuts or locking bolts to hold the rods apart at the distance needed to make the fabric taut. The fabric should be firm but not drum-tight; you should be able to press it gently without significant give, but not so tight that the weave distorts.

Lace the side edges of the fabric to the side bars of the frame with a strong thread or cord. This holds the width of the fabric even and prevents the edges from rolling inward. Thread the cord through the fabric edge every 2-3 cm and wrap it around the side bar.
Check the mounted fabric from the front. The
grid should be square, the threads running in straight horizontal and vertical lines. If the weave is diagonal, loosen one rod and re-mount more carefully.

items.symptom: The fabric sags in the middle of the frame
items.cause: The side lacing is missing or too loose.
items.fix: Lace the sides to the frame bars using a cord through the fabric edge and wrapped around the bar every 2-3 cm. This keeps the horizontal tension even across the full width.

items.symptom: The frame rods won't hold their position
items.cause: Wing-nuts are loose or the side bars have worn grooves.
items.fix: Tighten the wing-nuts firmly. If the frame is old and the locking mechanism is worn, place a small piece of rubber between the nut and the frame to increase friction.

content.text: Once the fabric is mounted, try stitching with both hands: one hand on top to place the needle and one underneath to return it. The scroll frame keeps the fabric stable enough to use both hands efficiently, which is faster than working with one hand and a hoop.
